# Incident Report — 2021-09-10 Traffic Analysis Exercise

## Victim host
- **IPv4:** 10.9.10.102
- **MAC:** 00:4f:49:b1:e8:c3
- **Windows hostname:** DESKTOP-KKITB6Q (domain-joined to `angrypoutine.com`, DC `ANGRYPOUTINE-DC`)
- **Logged-in user:** `hobart.gunnarsson` (seen in Kerberos `CNameString` across multiple AS-REQ/TGS-REQ exchanges with the domain controller 10.9.10.9)

## Malware family
**Attribution: behavioral, not signature-confirmed** (no Suricata/IDS alert file was present in the evidence directory — only the pcap was supplied).

Observed behavior chain:
1. HTTP GET to a bare domain hosting a PHP backend, using a randomized multi-segment URI and an MSIE7-on-Win10 spoofed User-Agent — a classic malware downloader/gate request pattern.
2. Server response disguised as a file download (`Content-Disposition: attachment; filename="date6"`) but the body is actually a raw **PE32+ DLL** (MZ/PE header confirmed), not the human-facing filename.
3. Within seconds, the host opens two TLS connections to unrelated external IPs, both presenting the **identical self-signed certificate** (CN/O/OU = `londonareloeli.uk` / `LL EST` / `UK System`, issued 2021-09-08, self-issued) — a hallmark of a malware family rotating C2 infrastructure behind boilerplate self-signed certs rather than legitimate CA-issued TLS.

This chain (bare-domain HTTP gate → disguised PE/DLL payload → immediate multi-host TLS beacon with shared self-signed cert) is consistent with a commodity Windows loader/banking-trojan family (e.g., Zloader/IcedID-style loader). Absent an IDS signature hit, the family name cannot be stated with certainty — it is reported here as **unidentified Windows DLL loader with self-signed-TLS C2**, behavioral attribution only.

## Indicators of Compromise (all grounded in the capture)

**C2 endpoints:**
- `194.62.42.206:80` — HTTP gate/delivery server (frame 1183–1246+, tcp.stream 50)
- `167.172.37.9:443` — TLS C2, self-signed cert CN `londonareloeli.uk` (tcp.stream 51, frame 1487 ClientHello, 1489 Certificate)
- `94.158.245.52:443` — TLS C2, identical self-signed cert CN `londonareloeli.uk` (frames 1842+)

**Malicious domain:**
- `simpsonsavingss.com` → resolved to 194.62.42.206 (DNS query/answer frame 1182; HTTP Host header frame 1189)

**Malicious URL:**
- `http://simpsonsavingss.com/bmdff/BhoHsCtZ/MLdmpfjaX/5uFG3Dz7yt/date1?BNLv65=pAAS` (frame 1189, GET request, User-Agent spoofed as MSIE 7.0)

**Transferred file:**
- Server-declared name: `date6` (Content-Disposition header, frame 1191 response headers)
- Actual file type: PE32+ DLL (GUI), x86-64
- **SHA256:** `eed363fc4af7a9070d69340592dcab7c78db4f90710357de29e3b624aa957cf8`
- Size: 284,816 bytes (Content-Length, frame 1191)

## Benign context (not indicators)
- Windows Update / Delivery Optimization traffic to `download.windowsupdate.com`, `au.download.windowsupdate.com`, `ctldl.windowsupdate.com` (23.1.237.x — Akamai)
- Microsoft telemetry/services: `v10.events.data.microsoft.com`, `login.live.com`, `settings-win.data.microsoft.com`, `nexus.officeapps.live.com`, msedge.net ring hosts, `store-images.s-microsoft.com`
- `www.msftncsi.com` / `dns.msftncsi.com` — Windows connectivity check
- `myexternalip.com` (34.117.59.81) — could be attacker recon (IP self-check) or benign network tool; traffic content not captured beyond DNS, so left as context rather than a hard IOC
- Internal AD/domain traffic: NBNS, LDAP/Kerberos/DCE-RPC/SMB to DC 10.9.10.9 and second workstation DESKTOP-MUYEYV7 (10.9.10.103)

## Incident summary
The Windows workstation DESKTOP-KKITB6Q (10.9.10.102, MAC 00:4f:49:b1:e8:c3), logged in as domain user `hobart.gunnarsson`, retrieved a disguised DLL payload (SHA256 `eed363fc...57cf8`) from the compromised/malicious site `simpsonsavingss.com` (194.62.42.206) over plain HTTP. Immediately afterward the host beaconed out over TLS to two separate IPs (167.172.37.9, 94.158.245.52) both presenting the same self-signed certificate for `londonareloeli.uk`, indicating the payload executed and established command-and-control. No IDS/Suricata alerts were provided alongside the pcap, so the malware family is named behaviorally rather than signature-confirmed.
